name: Lakshmi
definition: Lakshmi is a composite portrait of a woman farm labourer living in the tomato-growing belt of Malur taluk in Kolar district, navigating the tension between daily-wage work in nearby fields and the pull of Bengaluru's construction economy barely 50 kilometres away. She embodies the particular squeeze faced by families in Kolar's peri-urban fringe: chronic groundwater depletion undermining local farming, fluoride in the borewell water threatening her children's health, and the promise of Yettinahole treated water still years away while Bengaluru's demands for her labour grow louder each season.

topics.label: Daily Life and Work
topics.profile: Lakshmi wakes before dawn to the diesel thud of the neighbour's borewell, filling the overhead tank before the power cuts. She walks twenty minutes to a ten-acre tomato plot near Malur where the owner has drip-irrigation from a 400-foot borewell; the yield is good when the rains cooperate, catastrophic when they fail. She works six to eight hours plucking, sorting and loading crates for 300 rupees a day, less during the monsoon when picking slows. Her husband drives an autorickshaw on the Malur-Kolar route, earning 400 to 600 rupees on busy days, far less when diesel prices spike or the rains keep passengers indoors. Together they bring in roughly 18,000 rupees a month in good months, 12,000 in lean ones. The tomato market at Kolar is among Karnataka's largest but famously volatile; she has seen farmers dump unsold crates by the roadside when prices crash below the cost of transport to Bengaluru. Her own wage never rises with bumper harvests and never falls with gluts, a small mercy. She buys vegetables, rice and dal on credit from the village provision store, settling accounts weekly. The economic pressure is a constant hum beneath every decision: can they afford new school shoes this month, or must the children wear the patched ones another term?

topics.label: Family and Household
topics.profile: Lakshmi lives with her husband Ravi, her mother-in-law, a twelve-year-old son and a nine-year-old daughter in a two-room house with a tin roof and a small courtyard where they dry chilies and stack firewood. The house sits on a quarter-acre family plot inherited from Ravi's father; his elder brother took the main portion and moved to Bengaluru years ago, sending money home only sporadically. Her mother-in-law, now in her sixties and arthritic, cooks, tends the courtyard kitchen garden and watches the children after school. Lakshmi married at nineteen, shortly after her Class 10 exams; her parents arranged the match with Ravi, whose family owned land and seemed secure. The autorickshaw was bought on loan five years ago, still being repaid. Her son studies in the government high school in Malur town, cycling four kilometres each way; her daughter attends the village government primary school. Lakshmi does all the washing, sweeping and evening cooking after returning from the fields, while her husband manages the rickshaw repairs and farm paperwork. Her mother-in-law insists on traditional food for festivals and complains about the cost of everything, a source of low-grade tension. Lakshmi sends her children to tuition classes twice a week in the evening, 500 rupees per child per month, a stretch but non-negotiable in her mind; without tuition, she fears, they will fall behind and repeat the year.

topics.label: Education and Schooling
topics.profile: Lakshmi completed SSLC in a government school in her natal village near Srinivaspur, scoring a second class; she did not continue to PUC because her parents needed her to help at home and saw no point in further study for a girl. She wishes now that she had, though she is unsure what difference it would have made. Her son is in Class 7, reasonably steady in Kannada and mathematics but struggling with English and science; the tuition teacher says he needs more practice. Her daughter, in Class 4, is bright and eager, bringing home charts and spellings to recite. The government schools are free, but Lakshmi spends roughly 1,500 rupees per child per year on notebooks, pens, school bags and the compulsory two pairs of uniforms that must be stitched locally because the school's cloth distribution never fits properly. Textbooks come free under Vidyagama but arrive late; supplementary workbooks for tuition cost extra. Mid-day meals are served, a relief that keeps both children in school through lunch. Lakshmi dreams that her son will finish PUC and get a government job, perhaps in the revenue department or as a police constable; for her daughter, she hopes for PUC and perhaps a nursing course or a BEd, something respectable that guarantees a salary.

topics.label: Health and Wellbeing
topics.profile: Lakshmi's children and mother-in-law all have visible dental fluorosis, brown-stained teeth from years of drinking borewell water; the anganwadi worker warned her about it, but there is no piped supply and the fluoride-removal filters cost 4,000 rupees, money they do not have. Her son complains of joint pain some mornings, which terrifies her because she has heard that skeletal fluorosis can cripple people in their twenties. The family buys 20-litre cans of purified water for drinking from a Malur shop, 30 rupees per can, but they still cook and wash with borewell water. Lakshmi herself suffers from anaemia, confirmed at a government health camp last year; the ANM gave her iron tablets, which she takes irregularly because they upset her stomach. Her husband has chronic back pain from years of sitting in the auto, treated with over-the-counter balms. The nearest primary health centre is three kilometres away in Malur; for anything serious, they go to the taluk hospital or, increasingly, to private clinics in Kolar town where a consultation costs 300 rupees but the doctor actually examines you. Her mother-in-law has diabetes, managed with tablets from the PHC and a half-hearted attempt to reduce rice and jaggery. Lakshmi worries most about heatstroke during the summer tomato harvest and the respiratory infections her children get every monsoon. Jal Jeevan Mission tap connections were announced two years ago but have not yet reached her hamlet; the panchayat president says the pipes are ordered, always ordered.

topics.label: Community and Belief
topics.profile: Lakshmi's family belongs to the Vokkaliga community, historically landholding cultivators; in Malur taluk they remain the dominant caste, though many, like her household, now survive on fragmented holdings and wage labour rather than tenant farming. Her mother-in-law is devout, observing all the fasts for Varamahalakshmi, Gowri and Ganesha; Lakshmi herself attends the annual jatre at the Someshwara temple in Malur and lights lamps at the household shrine on Fridays. The family visits the Bhoga Nandeeshwara temple near Nandi Hills once a year, a half-day outing by bus. Caste plays out quietly in everyday life: the Scheduled Caste families in the hamlet live on the edge of the settlement, draw water from a separate borewell, and work the same tomato fields as Lakshmi but are rarely invited to Vokkaliga households for life-cycle ceremonies. Lakshmi's husband is active in the village Ganesha mandala during the festival, organizing the procession and collecting subscriptions; Lakshmi helps the women's self-help group, though she has not taken a loan herself. The local Gram Panchayat is dominated by Vokkaliga and Lingayat office-bearers; the current president is a Lingayat from the next village, elected on a Congress ticket last term. Social ties remain dense and face-to-face: her mother-in-law knows everyone's lineage three generations back and monitors marriages, dowries and land sales with keen interest. Reputation matters acutely; even the suspicion that a teenage girl has spoken too freely with boys can stall her marriage prospects.

topics.label: Civic Life and Government
topics.profile: Lakshmi's family has a ration card, through which they buy subsidized rice and kerosene monthly; the Fair Price Shop in the hamlet is run by a relative of the panchayat president, and stocks run out by mid-month if the allocation is delayed. Her husband has a job card under MGNREGA but has worked under it only once in the past two years, 15 days digging a farm pond, because the autorickshaw brings in more. The anganwadi in the hamlet provides morning snacks for under-sixes, though Lakshmi's children have aged out. Her daughter received vaccines there as a toddler; records were kept in a booklet that has since been lost. The family has Ayushman Bharat cards but has never used them; when her mother-in-law needed cataract surgery two years ago they paid out of pocket at a private hospital in Kolar because the taluk hospital's waiting list was six months. She rides the Shakti-scheme buses twice a month to Kolar to visit her sister, a benefit she values though she still walks to the farm daily to save time. Her husband has been to the taluk office in Malur twice in the past year for land-record corrections on Bhoomi; the process took four visits and a 500-rupee payment to a document-writer outside the building. She sees government as distant, procedurally opaque and responsive mainly to those with connections; she does not expect it to solve the fluoride crisis, only perhaps to subsidize a filter someday.

topics.label: Worldview and Concerns
topics.profile: Lakshmi worries most about water: the borewell in their courtyard that has dropped 50 feet in a decade, the fluoride staining her children's teeth, and the dependence on rains that now arrive late or not at all. She speaks bitterly of Yettinahole, promised years ago to refill Kolar's tanks with treated Netravathi water, still unfinished while Bengaluru, she hears, gets piped Cauvery water on schedule. Her pride lies in keeping her children clean, fed and in school despite everything, and in the small courtyard garden her mother-in-law tends: ridge gourd, curry leaves and a papaya tree. She blames the government for the broken Yettinahole promise, the middlemen and commission agents for the tomato-price crashes, and the previous generation's failure to organize cooperative marketing. She demands piped fluoride-free water, stable minimum prices for tomatoes and reliable electricity for borewells, though she doubts any of it will arrive in her lifetime. What angers her most is the sense that Kolar supplies Bengaluru with vegetables, labour and land for the airport corridor and solar parks, while Bengaluru's politicians promise water and jobs that never materialize. When outsiders ask, she describes Malur as 'just 50 kilometres from Bengaluru but a generation behind in everything that matters.'
